Connecting the Databricks Genie via MCP
This idx_01b5548f section covers everything required to make Databricks Genie available as a callable tool
inside the agent. Here you will go from confirming the prerequisites on the Databricks side,
configuring the MCP connection in Microsoft Foundry, completing the OAuth consent flow, to
verifying the tool returns correct data, and reviewing the exposed tool schema before building
the agent.
Confirm prerequisites on the Databricks side
Before creating idx_22f6420a the connection in Microsoft Foundry, confirm that the Databricks side is ready.
Managed MCP Servers must be enabled in the workspace, and the Genie space must be
published. You will also need the workspace hostname, Genie space ID, and full MCP endpoint
URL for the connection configuration steps that follow. Follow these steps to confirm and
collect those values:
In your Azure Databricks workspace, go to Settings > Previews
Find Managed MCP Servers in the list and confirm it is toggled On. If it is Off, enable
it and wait for the workspace to apply the change (typically happens in less than a
minute).
Navigate to Agents > MCP Servers in the Databricks workspace sidebar
Confirm your Genie space appears in the list of available managed MCP servers. Note
the MCP endpoint URL shown for the Genie space — it follows this format: https://
<workspace-hostname>/api/2.0/mcp/genie/<genie_space_id>
Open the Genie space and copy the Genie space ID from the browser URL. The ID is
the value after /genie/rooms/ in the URL https://<databricks-instance>/genie/
rooms/<space-id>
Save the following three values — you will need them for the next sections:
Workspace hostname: The instance name of your Databricks workspace (e.g.,
adb-1234567890.12.azuredatabricks.net)
Genie space ID: The value copied from the URL in the previous step
MCP endpoint URL: The full endpoint URL
The Databricks prerequisites are confirmed and the required values are saved. The next step is
to create the MCP connection in Microsoft Foundry.

Chapter 12 304
Configure the MCP connection
The idx_03c3875a MCP connection is what links Microsoft Foundry to the Databricks Genie space at the tool
level. Using Managed OAuth Identity Passthrough ensures the connector authenticates
through Microsoft Entra ID, which is the recommended approach for Azure Databricks
integrations—it avoids storing credentials and keeps access management centralized. Follow
these steps to configure the connection:
In Microsoft Foundry, ensure you are in the project retail-customer-assistant
In the Build tab, click Tools in the left pane
The Tools catalog opens. In the search bar at the top, type Azure Databricks Genie.
Click the Azure Databricks Genie card that appears in the results
Click Connect in the upper-right corner of the card. A connection configuration panel
opens on the right.
In the connection panel, fill in the following fields:
Name: genie ‑ retail ‑ purchases. This is the display name for the tool inside
Microsoft Foundry.
Remote MCP Server endpoint: This field is autopopulated by Foundry based on
the selected tool.
genie_space_id: Paste the Genie space ID copied before.
workspace-hostname: Enter the Databricks workspace instance name saved
before.
OAuth Identity Passthrough: Select Managed. This uses Microsoft Entra ID
authentication and is the recommended option for Azure Databricks.
Click Connect
Microsoft Foundry establishes the connection. Confirm the tool card for genie-retail-
purchases appears in the Tools list with a status indicator showing Connected.
The MCP connection is created. Before the agent can use it, you need to complete the OAuth
consent flow, which authorizes the connection to call the Databricks Genie space on behalf of
your organization's account.
OAuth consent flow
The idx_b355ad0f OAuth consent flow is a one-time authorization step. Microsoft Foundry triggers it the first
time it attempts to call the Genie tool — you will see a consent link appear in the playground
response, which you click to authenticate with Databricks. Once approved, the connection

Building the agent
This section walks through the full agent configuration: creating the agent, selecting the
model, writing the system prompt that governs identity handling, data minimization, tool
routing, and escalation behavior, connecting the Genie tool, appending routing instructions,
and verifying the agent in the playground. Complete the subsections in order — the tool
routing instructions reference the Genie tool, which must be connected before the instructions
are added.
Create the agent
Creating the idx_422c9e5b agent in the portal establishes the container for everything that follows. The
name and description you set here are what appear in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center and in
the Teams app store when the agent is published, so use names that are meaningful to end
users. Follow these steps:
Click on the Build tab in the main menu, then click Agents in the left pane
Click + Create agent
In the Agent name field, enter retail ‑ customer ‑ assistant

Chapter 12 308
In the Description field, enter Customer ‑ facing agent that answers questions
about retail store activity, purchase history, and loyalty points using
Databricks Genie
Click Create
The idx_c74774f8 agent is created. The next step is to select the deployed model and write the system
prompt that defines how the agent behaves across every customer interaction.
Model configuration
The idx_31736117 system prompt is the behavioral contract for the agent. It tells the model when to answer
from its instructions, when to call the Genie tool, how to handle missing customer identifiers,
what to say when no data is found, and what it must never do. For a customer-facing retail
assistant, the system prompt is as important as any technical configuration — a vague or
incomplete prompt produces inconsistent behavior that no guardrail can fully compensate for.
Follow these steps to configure the model and paste the system prompt:
Inside the agent editor, locate the Model section
In the Deployment dropdown, select gpt-4.1-retail (deployed in Creating the basics
section)
Leave all other model parameters at their defaults
In the Instructions field, clear any default placeholder text
Paste the following system prompt exactly as written:
You are a customer support assistant for a retail store.
You help customers with questions about their purchase history and loyalty
points.
Your role:
- Answer general questions about the loyalty program conversationally.
- For any question about the customer's personal data (purchases, points,
transactions, spending totals), you MUST call the ask_genie tool.
- Never answer personal data questions from memory or assumptions.
Identity handling:
- Before calling ask_genie, confirm the customer has provided their loyalty
ID
or registered email address.
- If no identifier is present, respond with:
'To look that up, I'll need your loyalty ID or registered email.
Could you please share that?'

chunks.content:
5.309 Building an Agent that Uses Databricks Genie via MCP
- Do not attempt a tool call without a valid customer identifier.
Rules you must always follow:
- Only return data fields directly relevant to the customer's question.
Do not expose the full dataset returned by the tool.
- If the tool returns no results, respond with:
'I wasn't able to find any data for that account.
Please verify your loyalty ID or email and try again.'
- If the tool call fails, respond with:
'I'm having trouble retrieving that information right now.
Please try again in a moment or contact support.'
- Never invent, estimate, or extrapolate customer data.
- Never discuss other customers' data.
- Do not process refunds, adjust points, or modify any account data.
- Do not browse external websites.
Hybrid questions:
- If a question has both a general part and a personal data part, answer
the general part first from your instructions, then call ask_genie
for the personal data part in the same response.
Example: 'How do I earn points, and how many do I have?'
→ Explain the earning rules, then call the tool for the balance.
Response format:
- Keep responses concise and conversational.
- Summarize tool results in plain language. Do not paste raw data.
- For lists (e.g., last three purchases), use a simple formatted list.
- For numeric values (e.g., points balance), state the number clearly
and include the last-updated date if available.
Click Save in the upper-right corner of the agent editor
The system idx_814af09c prompt above defines five behavioral layers: identity gating (the agent must
confirm a customer identifier before any tool call), data minimization (return only the fields
relevant to the question), tool routing (all personal data questions go to ask_genie), error
handling (explicit responses for no-data and tool-failure scenarios), and scope enforcement
(no refunds, no point adjustments, no external browsing). Each layer maps directly to a risk
that would arise in production without it.
The model is idx_34908700 configured and the system prompt is saved. The next step is to connect the Genie
tool to the agent so it can make live calls to the Databricks Genie space.

Chapter 12 310
Connect the Databricks genie tool
Connecting idx_62f9a770 the Genie tool to the agent is what makes the system prompt's routing instructions
executable. Without this connection, any ask_genie call in the system prompt will fail — the
agent needs an active, authorized tool to invoke. Setting the approval mode to Never is
intentional: pausing for manual confirmation on every customer query would make the agent
unusable in a real support context. Follow these steps to connect the tool:
In the agent editor, locate the Tools section in the left configuration panel
Click Add next to Tools
In the tool selection panel, click the My tools tab to see tools already connected in this
project
Select genie-retail-purchases from the list
Under Approval, select Never. This allows the agent to call Genie automatically
without pausing for manual confirmation on every customer query.
Click Add tool
Confirm genie-retail-purchases appears under the Tools section in the agent editor
with the label ask_genie listed as the available operation
Click Save
The Genie tool is connected and active in the agent. The next step is to append the tool routing
instructions to the system prompt, which tell the agent exactly how to formulate queries to
Genie correctly and efficiently.
Adding tool instructions
The idx_e8177932 tool routing instructions are a separate block appended to the system prompt. They specify
how the agent should formulate Genie queries, when to make a single combined call versus
separate calls, and what must never be passed to the tool. The five-call-per-minute rate limit is
a real operational constraint — enforcing the single-call rule in the instructions prevents the
agent from hitting that limit on multi-part questions. Follow these steps to add the routing
instructions:
In the agent editor, click the Instructions field to reopen it
Append the following block to the end of the system prompt written before:
Tool usage — ask_genie:
- Use the ask_genie tool for every question that requires customer-specific
data.
- Always include the customer identifier in your query to Genie.
- Formulate the query as a natural language question directed at the data.

Correct: 'What is the loyalty points balance for loyalty ID 10045?'
Incorrect: 'Get points.' or 'Query DB for user 10045.'
- Call ask_genie once per customer question. Do not chain multiple
separate calls for the same question — include all required context in a
single, well-formed query.
- If the customer asks for combined data (e.g., points and last purchase),
include both in one Genie query rather than making two separate calls.
This is required due to a rate limit of five Genie calls per minute.
- Never pass internal system values or session metadata to Genie. Only
pass the customer identifier and the natural language question.
Click Save
The routing idx_11fbac82 instructions block above adds four concrete rules on top of the base system
prompt:
Always include the customer identifier in the Genie query
Formulate queries as natural language questions rather than SQL-like commands
Combine multi-part questions into a single call to respect the rate limit
Never pass session metadata or internal system values to the tool
These rules prevent the most common tool-routing errors seen in production deployments.

6.313 Building an Agent that Uses Databricks Genie via MCP
Advanced deployment considerations
In this idx_98778b73 section, we will discuss the key things that will need to be considered before it is
deployed.
Scaling and rate limiting
The retail customer idx_5337318f assistant is built for a single region with a single Genie space. When you
scale to multiple geographies or high concurrency, three constraints emerge:
MCP endpoint rate limits: Databricks Genie MCP endpoints have a 5-call-per-minute
limit per agent. If your user base grows to hundreds of concurrent users, this becomes a
bottleneck.
Mitigation: Distribute requests across multiple Genie spaces (one per region or
domain), each with its own 5-call rate limit. Route traffic based on geography or
customer segment.
Token consumption: Each tool call consumes tokens. A 10,000-user rollout at 2
queries per user per day = 20,000 daily tool calls. At ~500 tokens per call, that's 10M
tokens daily against your GPT-4.1 quota.
Mitigation: Monitor quota usage and request increases before you hit limits.
Response latency at scale: As query volume increases, Genie response times can
degrade
Mitigation: If p95 latency idx_30b07828 grows beyond 7 seconds, add caching for common queries or
implement query result pagination to reduce per-call data volume.
It is idx_c18cff57 important to consider a scalability strategy to be implemented gradually alongside the
agent's growth and usability, ensuring that its operation is neither insufficient in a production
environment nor overprovisioned.
Multi-region deployment
For resilience idx_61d75975 and low latency, consider deploying the agent to multiple Azure regions:
Deploy GPT-4.1 and the agent configuration to each region.
Keep a single Genie space in the primary region but replicate read-only snapshots to
secondary regions for failover.
Use Azure Traffic Manager to route requests by geography or fail over to secondary
regions if the primary is unavailable.
Each region's agent has its own managed identity with RBAC permission to its local
Genie copy. This prevents a single RBAC change from breaking all regions.

Chapter 12 314
Evaluate your primary audience and its geographic location. This will provide insight into
potential future expansion regions to enhance the solution's high availability and bring it
closer to the largest group of users.
Disaster recovery and fallback
Production idx_21677c97 failures happen. Plan for them:
Genie space unavailable: System prompt tells the agent to respond with " I'm having
trouble retrieving that information right now. " This is correct, but users see
degraded service. Set up a read-only cache of the previous 7 days of Genie responses. If
the live Genie space is unavailable for more than 5 minutes, switch to the cache for
reads. This keeps service available for recent queries while you fix Genie.
Foundry region unavailable: If the Azure region hosting your agent goes down,
failover to a secondary region. This requires pre-deployment of the agent to the
secondary region and Traffic Manager configured to detect unavailability and redirect
within 30 seconds.
Managed identity misconfigured: Happens after Azure RBAC changes. Every Genie idx_ce5f5109
call fails. Response: immediately roll back the RBAC change (keep a record of the
previous state) or re-run the RBAC assignment script. Response SLA: 15 minutes.
Monitor 403 errors and alert immediately.
Operational runbooks
Create a runbook idx_8d7d7da6 for each failure mode:
Tool calls failing (>5% error rate): Check Genie MCP status → Check agent managed
identity RBAC → Check Databricks workspace availability → Check quota/rate limits.
Response time: 15 minutes.
Empty result spike (>15% of queries): Check Genie space row-level security
configuration → Check query logs for errors → Verify data is present in Genie.
Response time: 30 minutes.
Latency spike (p95 > 9 seconds): Check Genie slow query logs → Check agent
concurrency limits → Check if Databricks compute is scaled appropriately. Response
time: 20 minutes.
Document idx_1ddffe82 these runbooks in your team wiki and link them from your alert rules. When an
alert fires, engineers know exactly what to check first. Before the agent can be considered ready
for deployment, it must pass a structured evaluation that tests its behavior across the full
range of scenarios it will encounter in production.

Once completed, review the results against the deployment thresholds in the next section.
Review evaluation results
The review idx_98573c2f step is a gate, not a formality. Each threshold below reflects the minimum
acceptable quality level for an agent that handles live customer data in a retail context. Follow
these steps to review the results:
Click on retail-eval-run-01 to open the results
In the Metrics dashboard, review the aggregate scores. The following minimum
thresholds must be met before deployment:
Task adherence: ≥ 4 out of 5
Groundedness: ≥ 4 out of 5
Relevance: ≥ 4 out of 5
Intent resolution: ≥ 80% pass rate
Tool call accuracy: ≥ 90% pass rate — higher threshold than the vehicle guide
because incorrect tool routing in a live customer context has direct data privacy
implications
All safety evaluators: 0 flagged rows
Click the Per-sample metrics tab. Filter results by the category column to review each
scenario group separately.
For any identity_handling row where Task adherence scores are below 3, the agent
called Genie without confirming an identifier. Return to the system prompt and
strengthen the identity check instruction.
For any hybrid_question row where the Tool call accuracy shows Fail, open the tool
call log and count the number of Genie calls. If more than one call was made, the agent
split the combined query. Return to the tool instructions section and reinforce the
single-call rule.
For any out_of_scope or security row where Task adherence scores below 3, verify
the guardrail section is correctly assigned, and the blocklist entries are saved
For any no_data_edge_case row where Groundedness scores below 3, check whether
the agent returned a fabricated value when Genie returned empty results. Tighten the
no-data response rule in the system prompt.

6.7 319 Building an Agent that Uses Databricks Genie via MCP
After this, all idx_d370f748 evaluation thresholds should be met and the agent is ready for deployment. The
next section covers publishing the agent, reassigning the Databricks MCP access to the new
agent identity, enabling tracing, and approving the agent in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center.
Deploying and monitoring in production
This section idx_59b5e763 covers the deployment steps required to take the agent from validated to live in
production: publishing to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot, reassigning the Databricks
workspace RBAC to the agent's managed identity, enabling Application Insights tracing, and
approving the agent in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center. Complete these steps in order—
skipping the RBAC reassignment means Genie calls will fail in production even though the
playground worked correctly.
Publish the agent
Publishing idx_e94b74be the agent registers it with Azure Bot Service and makes it available for distribution
through Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Save the Application ID and Tenant ID that are
generated — you will need both in the next step to grant the agent's managed identity access
to the Databricks workspace. Follow these steps:
Click on the Build tab in the main menu, then click Agents, and then retail-customer-
assistant
Select the agent version that passed all evaluation thresholds
Click Publish Agent
In the publishing dialog, click Publish again, then select Publish to Teams and
Microsoft 365 Copilot
In the Microsoft 365 publishing window:
Under Azure Bot Service, select Create an Azure Bot Service
Under Distribution scope, select Organization
Note the Application ID and Tenant ID generated. Save both values.
Click Publish. Wait for status Published to appear (1–2 minutes).
The agent idx_2cdabee1 is published and the Application ID and Tenant ID are saved. Publishing creates a
managed identity for the agent that does not yet have permission to call the Databricks MCP
endpoint — that is what the RBAC reassignment covers next.
Reassign RBAC for the Databricks MCP connection
When idx_8f6ed5fa the agent was tested in the playground, it called Genie using your personal Azure
account. Now that it is published, it uses a system-assigned managed identity tied to the Azure
Bot Service application. That identity needs Contributor access on the Databricks workspace

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 320
chunks.content:
Chapter 12 320
resource to invoke the MCP endpoint at runtime. Without this, every Genie call in production
will return a 403 Forbidden error. Follow these steps:
In the Azure portal (https://portal.azure.com), navigate to your A zure Databricks
workspace resource
Click Access control (IAM), click + Add, and then Add role assignment
In the Role dropdown, select Contributor. This grants the published agent identity
permission to call the Databricks MCP endpoint.
Under Members, click + Select members. Search for the Application ID saved before
and select it.
Click Review + assign. Confirm the assignment appears in the Role assignments tab.
Return to Microsoft Foundry, click on the Build tab, then click Tools, and then genie-
retail-purchases
Verify the tool status still shows Connected. If it shows Error or Unauthorized, re-
trigger the OAuth consent flow from the tool detail view by clicking Reconnect.
The idx_120f1024 Databricks RBAC assignment is complete and the tool connection is verified. The next step
is to enable tracing so that every production interaction is recorded and available for analysis.
Enable tracing and monitoring
Tracing idx_e0daa5bf sends every conversation turn, tool call, and guardrail annotation to Application
Insights where you can query, alert on, and visualize them. For a retail assistant handling
customer data, this gives you the operational visibility to detect anomalies early — unusual
tool call failure rates, unexpected escalation patterns, or groundedness drops that might
indicate the Genie space schema has changed. Follow these steps to enable tracing:
Click on Operate tab in the main menu, then in the left pane click Tracing
Click Enable tracing for retail-customer-assistant
Under Destination, select Application Insights
Select an existing Application Insights instance or click Create new and accept the
defaults
Click Save
Tracing is enabled, but enabling it is not the same as having visibility. Systems can run
"successfully" while quietly degrading — returning stale data, hitting rate limits, or timing out
without surfacing errors. Understanding what can go wrong is what separates a system you
operate from one that operates you.

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.content:
3.4 5.
321 Building an Agent that Uses Databricks Genie via MCP
Operational challenges and degradation patterns in
production
A idx_c9731846 production agent depends on several moving parts, including the MCP connection,
Databricks availability, managed identity permissions, schema stability, guardrail behavior,
and monitoring pipelines. Even when the agent appears to be running successfully, issues such
as timeouts, stale data, empty results, or schema changes can slowly degrade the customer
experience.
In this section, we will look at the most common operational challenges you should plan for
after deployment. You will learn how to handle transient failures, identify issues that require
manual intervention, detect silent degradation patterns that may not appear as obvious errors,
and define the operational signals your team should monitor. This will help you move beyond
simply publishing the agent and toward running it reliably in a production environment.
Retry strategies and transient failures
The MCP idx_f8ccbfed connection to Genie is not guaranteed to succeed on the first attempt. Foundry retries
once with exponential backoff for transient issues. However, three patterns require different
handling:
Timeouts: If Genie queries exceed 10 seconds, the connection times out. A sudden
spike in timeouts suggests either larger dataset scans or Databricks degradation. Alert
if timeouts exceed 5% of Genie calls in 5 minutes.
Authentication failures: If the agent's managed identity loses RBAC permission, every
call fails with 403. Manual RBAC remediation required. Monitor for 403 errors and
respond within the hour.
Schema mismatches: If Databricks changes the Genie schema (field renamed,
removed), tool calls fail silently or return partial data. Your first signal might be a
customer complaint, not an error log. Run a weekly schema validation test with a
known query to verify expected fields are returned.
Having a idx_452118b5 retry strategy is important since any connection depends on a successful response to
start sending data so the complete agent workflow can continue operating without
interruptions or incomplete data.
•
•
•

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 322
chunks.content:
Chapter 12 322
Silent degradation patterns
Three idx_c18bb3b3 failure modes look like success in logs:
Stale data: If Genie is not refreshed regularly, responses are correct-looking but
outdated. Monitor timestamp fields in responses — if they're older than 24 hours,
investigate the data refresh pipeline.
Empty results: Genie succeeds but returns zero rows. If this happens for 10% of valid
loyalty IDs, the Genie scope may be incomplete. This won't show as errors — you have
to ask why so many valid requests return nothing.
Response truncation: Large purchase histories get silently truncated to fit response
limits. Monitor Genie result sizes — if the 95th percentile approaches your limit,
increase it or add pagination.
In these cases, focus on these operational signals (these are not the only ones to review, but
they are a starting point):
Tool call success rate: Target ≥ 95%. Drops indicate authentication, Databricks issues,
or timeouts.
No-data response rate: Baseline in week one. Spikes suggest scope problems or data
sync issues.
Response latency p95/p99: Alert if approaching 8-9 seconds (timeout threshold is
10s).
Data freshness: Alert if max timestamp is older than 24 hours.
Guardrail activation rate: Spikes suggest behavioral change or misconfiguration.
Set thresholds idx_ae4166d6 as change indicators, not absolutes: if success rate drops 5% from baseline, alert.
Changes matter more than absolute values because they vary by time and seasonality.
The operational posture
The idx_e8696434 following timeline should be kept in mind:
Week one: Baseline everything
Week two: Set thresholds 5–10% looser than baseline
Week three: Detect degradation early
Ensure production discipline, i.e., listening to signals, responding to patterns, and adjusting
configurations, to keep the system healthy long-term.
After reviewing the operational challenges and degradation patterns that can affect a
production deployment, we now have a clearer picture of what must be monitored once the
agent is live. The final step is to control how the agent is released to users. Instead of making it
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
323 Building an Agent that Uses Databricks Genie via MCP
available to the entire organization immediately, we will approve it through the Microsoft 365
Admin Center and limit the initial rollout to specific users or groups. This gives the team a safer
way to validate real-world usage, observe production signals, and respond quickly if any issues
appear during the first days of deployment.
Approving the agent in Microsoft 365 Admin Center
The idx_520b60bc Microsoft 365 Admin Center approval is the last gate before end users can interact with the
agent. Until this step is completed, the agent is published at the Azure level but not yet
distributed to any user. Selecting Specific users or groups for the initial rollout — rather than

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 322
chunks.content:
the full organization — is standard practice for a first production deployment: it limits the
blast radius if an unexpected issue surfaces in the first days of live traffic. Follow these steps:
Open the Microsoft 365 Admin Center (https://admin.microsoft.com).
Navigate to Settings, then Integrated apps
Locate retail-customer-assistant in the pending approvals list
Click the agent name and then Deploy
Under Users, select Specific users or groups and add those who will be using the
agent
Click Finish deployment
Now we idx_e3d9ddce have a fully functional agent connected to a Databricks Genie space through MCP.
This solution operates in a real production environment. We can add more configurations to
the solutions as well as deploy them in different locations for an omnichannel architecture
approach.
Summary
Let's recap. Starting from a clearly scoped use case, we set up a Microsoft Foundry project for a
retail customer assistant, deployed a GPT-4.1 model, and established the workspace that
would support everything built on top of it. We then connected a Databricks Genie space to the
agent through the Model Context Protocol, configuring the OAuth consent flow and verifying
that the tool returned structured customer data — purchase history, loyalty points, and
spending totals — before a single line of agent logic was written. With that foundation in
place, we built the agent itself. The agent was then hardened with a custom guardrail covering
content harms, prompt injection, sensitive data exposure, groundedness, and task adherence
at the tool call level, alongside a blocklist that blocks out-of-scope requests.
Then we use an evaluation dataset for testing different types of cases such as correct tool
routing, identity handling, accurate Genie calls, response formatting, edge case handling, and

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 324
chunks.content:
Chapter 12 324
out-of-scope refusal. Results were reviewed by category, with specific remediation paths
mapped to each failure type, and runs were compared across iterations to confirm measurable
improvement before deployment.
Finally, the agent was published to Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot, RBAC was
reassigned to the newly published identity on the Databricks workspace, and Application
Insights was connected to monitor tool call rates, error rates, and groundedness in production.
The result is an agent that retrieves live customer data from Databricks Genie safely, reliably,
and within clearly defined boundaries.
Completing this chapter marks the end of the book. Over the course of the last three chapters,
you built three production-grade AI agents applying the different concepts and techniques
described in this book. Now you are ready to start designing AI solutions from the concept up
to the production implementation using Microsoft Foundry.
